newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian leu stable but long-term trend unclear.
newsitem.headline: Romanian leu stable but long-term trend unclear.

text.p: Romania's leu currency has gained a measure of stability over the past month, benefiting from tough monetary policies and fresh foreign inflows, but analysts are reluctant to forecast a long-term trend.
"What seems to be certain is that the leu will not shift significantly in the next few months," said one local dealer.
The leu opened on Thursday at 7,040/80 to the dollar, little changed on a market unmoved by Wednesday's news that the International Monetary Fund had approved $430 million in loans.

Romania's financial markets appear little affected by news which would have a significant influence on currencies and stocks elsewhere, including economic indicators such as inflation or bank reserves.

This week central bank (BNR) governor Mugur Isarescu said tightened monetary policy and increased dollar inflows after year-old restrictions were lifted on the currency market in February had pulled the leu out of a steep plunge.

Inflows generated by exports and higher foreign investments have made the market dollar-heavy, prompting the BNR to soak up the excess to prevent a rise in the leu which would be harmful to exporters.
"We have to support the greenback, having in mind the large inflows of hard currency on our market," said Isarescu.
Foreign direct investments in Romania were up 35 percent in the first quarter from the same period of 1996.
The overall figure of more than $2.3 billion since the fall of communism in 1989 is low among ex-communist countries in eastern Europe.
Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea said the IMF approval, the focal point of the new centrist government's programme, lent credibility to reforms and opened the door for new investment.
Among the accord's targets are lower inflation and higher exchange reserves.
The deal to resume loans was clinched a year after the IMF suspended credits to the government's leftist predecessor, thrown out of office last November.
Bucharest has pledged a flexible exchange rate policy to stimulate exports and narrow the current account deficit to $1.4 billion this year from $2.3 billion in 1996.
Fund money and dollar purchases from the local market are expected to push the BNR's foreign reserves up to about $2 billion in June or July from a current $1.1 billion.

Analysts said portfolio investors were scanning equity and debt markets for the right moment to invest more. Many decisions hinged on an expansion in securities trading and rules clarifying profit repatriation.
"With that money ready to rush in, we might witness some pressure which could push up the leu," said one analyst.
Dollar sentiment was also depressed by a "leu hunger" earlier this year which pulled the dollar back from all-time highs of 9,000 lei in February. At the New Year it had stood at 4,100.
"One of the key issues facing policy makers will be how to keep the leu declining in line with inflation and competitive for exporters," Morgan Stanley's Eric Fine said from London.
Monthly inflation hit an all-time high of 30.7 percent in March after price liberalisation pushed first-quarter inflation to 76.5 percent.
Romania has undertaken to slow monthly inflation to about 2.0 percent by the end of 1997 and to reach a year-on-year target of 90 percent, now seen to be all but out of reach.
"The timing of any depreciation is difficult to forecast," a London analyst said. "Any unsustainable real firming in the next few months might be reversed later in the year."

Some economists said a falling leu would not tackle the country's bulging trade gap. They said higher exports, after a 3.2 percent drop in 1996, were linked to a change in the structure of the economy.
